+# How the Ropewalk Carries a Fifty-Fathom Order
+
+## What happens
+
+The customer's asking passes through five moments, each held in a different module, until it stands complete in the dispatch book.
+
+**1. The counter takes the order (counter.py)**
+
+The clerk at the counter calls `take_order(yard, "Trelawney", 50, "hawser")`. The counter validates that "hawser" is a lay the walk is rigged for (line 18 in counter.py lists STRANDS; hawser has 3 strands) and that 50 is at least one fathom. It then calculates how many complete hauls the walk must make. A haul is one trip down the walk, fixed at 20 fathoms (line 15). The counter uses ceiling division: `hauls_for(50) = -(-50 // 20) = 3` (line 28). So three hauls will happen, walking `3 × 20 = 60` fathoms total.
+
+**2. The walk draws from the rack (walk.py and stores.py)**
+
+The counter calls `walk.walk_out(yard, 60, 3, "hawser")` (line 41 in counter.py). The walk calculates the raw yarn needed: each strand of a hawser lay runs the full length, so `yarn_for(60, 3) = 60 × 3 = 180` fathoms (line 19 in walk.py). The walk then checks that the rack holds at least 180 fathoms—if not, the order is refused whole and the rack is left untouched (lines 30-34 in walk.py).
+
+If the rack has enough, the walk calls `stores.draw(yard, 180)` (line 35 in walk.py). The `draw` function on the rack (stores.py, line 42) removes bundles from the front, the order they were put up. It empties each bundle completely before touching the next. If a bundle has more yarn than is left to draw, the bundle shrinks in place at the front; otherwise, it comes off the rack entirely and the next bundle moves forward. `draw` returns the mark (identifier) of every bundle it touched—in the order touched, with repetitions if the draw spanned part of a bundle and then came back to it (though a bundle touched twice is a bundle left in the middle, so it appears only once in practice because `draw` leaves remainder bundles at the front and moves on).
+
+**3. The coil is formed (walk.py)**
+
+`walk_out` returns a coil object (line 36–41 in walk.py) that holds:
+- `"fathoms": 60` — the length the walk laid (the three hauls)
+- `"lay": "hawser"` — the lay pattern used
+- `"yarn_fathoms": 180` — the raw yarn consumed (60 × 3)
+- `"bundles": drawn` — the marks of every bundle the draw touched
+
+**4. The book receives the entry (book.py)**
+
+The counter calls `book.enter(yard, "Trelawney", 50, coil)` (line 42 in counter.py). The book assigns the coil a tag by taking the next serial number from the yard (line 13 in book.py: `yard["next_serial"]` is read and then incremented), and formats it as `"RW-N"` where N is the serial (line 25). 
+
+The book then appends a dispatch record to `yard["dispatches"]` (lines 26–35 in book.py):
+- `"tag": "RW-1"` (or whatever the next serial is)
+- `"customer": "Trelawney"`
+- `"asked": 50` — what the customer asked for at the counter
+- `"walked": 60` — what the walk actually laid (the coil's fathoms)
+- `"lay": "hawser"`
+- `"price_pence": 60 × 9 = 540` — charged at 9 pence per fathom for hawser (line 8 in book.py), but charged for the walked length, not the asked length
+
+The book returns the tag to the counter, which returns it to `cli.py` (line 30 in cli.py), which prints it as output.
+
+**5. The yard is saved (cli.py and stores.py)**
+
+After the entire order is taken, `cli.py` calls `stores.save(yard, args.yard)` (line 47 in cli.py). This writes the whole yard—bundles, dispatches, and next serial—as JSON to disk (stores.py, line 27), so the record persists.
+
+## Why it comes out that way
+
+The mechanism enforces several design choices, each load-bearing:
+
+**Hauls are whole.** A haul is 20 fathoms (line 15 in counter.py), and the walk cannot lay less than a full haul. The counter uses `hauls_for` to round up: an asking of 50 fathoms is 2.5 hauls, so it becomes 3 hauls = 60 fathoms walked. The customer asked for 50 but receives 60; the counter never sends a customer away short (line 26, the comment in `hauls_for`). This is a business choice: the walk's rigging is fixed, so partial hauls are not economical.
+
+**The walk is all-or-nothing.** Before any yarn comes off the rack, the walk checks that the entire need can be met (lines 30–34 in walk.py). This is an atomic decision: either the order is taken whole, or it fails and the rack is untouched. If an order calls for 180 fathoms and only 175 are on hand, the walk raises an error and no dispatch entry is made. The module that makes this decision (walk.py) does not touch the rack directly—it delegates to `stores.draw`—but it checks first, so `draw` never fails.
+
+**Bundles come off in order.** The rack is FIFO: bundles are put up at the back (line 34 in stores.py, `append`) and drawn from the front (line 55 in stores.py, `yard["bundles"][0]`). A bundle drawn partway stays at the front with its remainder (line 58 in stores.py, `bundle["fathoms"] -= left`). This means yarn is consumed in the order it was delivered—first in, first out—so the first bundles to arrive are the first to be spun into rope.
+
+**Strands multiply the walk's take.** A hawser has 3 strands (line 18 in counter.py), and every strand runs the full 60 fathoms walked. So the walk takes 180 fathoms off the rack to lay 60 fathoms of rope (line 19 in walk.py: `yarn_for(60, 3) = 60 × 3`). The coil records both figures: "fathoms" (what the customer gets) and "yarn_fathoms" (what the walk consumed). The price is charged on the coil's fathoms—the walked length—not the input length (line 33 in book.py). A hawser-laid rope costs 9 pence per fathom (line 8 in book.py), so 60 fathoms = 540 pence, regardless of what was asked. The walk's efficiency is hidden from the invoice; the customer pays for the rope they receive, not the yarn the walk burned.
+
+**The asking and the walked are both recorded.** The dispatch entry keeps both `"asked": 50` and `"walked": 60` (lines 30–31 in book.py). This is the record of what was asked and what was paid for. If a customer disputes a bill, the book shows the lay, the asking, the walked length, and the price—all the facts needed to settle it.
+
+**The serial number steps automatically.** Each coil gets the next serial in sequence, and the serial increments as soon as it is taken (lines 13–14 in book.py, `take_serial`). This is done inside the book module before the dispatch is written, so every coil that makes it to the book gets a unique, sequential tag. If the order fails at the walk (not enough yarn), no serial is taken and no entry is made; the next order will take the same serial that this one was refused.
+
+## Boundaries and edge behavior
+
+**Insufficient yarn on the rack.** If fewer than 180 fathoms are on hand when the order reaches the walk, `walk.walk_out` raises `ValueError` with a message showing how many fathoms the rack holds and how many the walk needs (lines 31–34 in walk.py). The exception is raised before `stores.draw` is called, so the rack is untouched. Control returns to `cli.py`, the exception propagates, and the order is not taken. No serial is taken from the book, no dispatch is written, and the yard is not saved. The next order will start from the same state as before.
+
+**Insufficient fathoms requested.** `take_order` rejects any asking less than 1 fathom (line 39 in counter.py). `put_up` rejects any bundle less than 1 fathom (line 33 in stores.py). This is a boundary that prevents empty orders and empty bundles.
+
+**An unknown lay.** If the customer asks for a lay not in `STRANDS`—say, "cable" when only "hawser" and "shroud" are rigged—`take_order` raises `ValueError` (lines 36–37 in counter.py). The order fails before the walk is reached.
+
+**A partial bundle at the front of the rack.** When `draw` runs, it may encounter a bundle that does not have enough fathoms to meet the remaining demand. For example, if 180 fathoms are needed and the front bundle has 75, the bundle comes off empty and the draw moves to the next bundle (line 62 in stores.py, `pop(0)`). If the front bundle has 200 fathoms and only 180 are left to draw, the bundle stays at the front with 20 fathoms remaining (line 58 in stores.py, `bundle["fathoms"] -= left`). In both cases, the bundle's mark is added to the list returned by `draw` (line 56). So the coil's "bundles" field records every bundle that `draw` touched, even if only a small amount came off that bundle.
+
+**Rounding up creates surplus yarn.** The customer asked for 50 fathoms and received 60. But the walk walked 60, so the coil is 60 fathoms long and is billed at 60 × 9 = 540 pence. The surplus (10 fathoms) is paid for by the customer. The mechanism builds this in: hauls are indivisible, so any order that is not an exact multiple of 20 fathoms overshoots. The counter's `hauls_for` function makes this choice explicit (line 26 in counter.py, the comment). There is no mechanism to sell the leftover—it stays on the coil. The cost is borne by the customer.
+
+**The walk's strands are hidden from the asking.** The customer orders a lay, not a strand count. `take_order` maps "hawser" to 3 strands (line 41 in counter.py), and the walk uses this to calculate yarn needed (line 19 in walk.py). But the ordering interface does not expose strand count; the customer says "hawser-laid" and that is enough. The strands are a property of the lay, set once and used every time.
+
+**The dispatch book is append-only.** New coils are appended to `yard["dispatches"]` (line 26 in book.py), never inserted, removed, or reordered. This means the dispatch book grows monotonically, and the order of entries reflects the order in which coils left the yard. There is no mechanism to cancel, refund, or edit a dispatch once it is written.
+
+**The yarn file is the sole state.** Everything—the rack, the book, and the next serial—lives in one JSON file (stores.py, line 15, `YARD_FILE = "yard.json"`). There is no separate database, no log file, no backup. If the file is corrupted, the state is lost. If two clerks run orders at the same time, the last one to save wins and the earlier one's changes are overwritten. The mechanism assumes a single clerk and a single machine, not concurrent access.
